title: Effective ultimate-positivity thresholds for simple recurrences
formal: Is there a single deterministic Turing machine that, given any simple rational linear recurrence sequence \((u_n)_{n\ge0}\), always halts and returns either \(\mathrm{NO}\), meaning that the sequence is not ultimately nonnegative, or a natural number \(N\) satisfying \[\forall n\ge N,\qquad u_n\ge0?\] It must return \(\mathrm{NO}\) exactly when \(\forall N\in\mathbb N\ \exists n\ge N:u_n<0\). A valid natural-number output may be any sufficient threshold; it need not be the smallest one. The input recurrence length is unrestricted. Equivalently, because Ultimate Positivity for simple recurrences is already decidable, ask for a procedure that halts and outputs such a threshold on every ultimately nonnegative simple input, with no condition on other inputs.
why: This problem isolates a precise gap between deciding an eventual property and computing a point after which it holds. An effective bound would make the exceptional prefix finite and accessible and would decide all-time Positivity for simple recurrences. The difference matters whenever an eventual mathematical guarantee must become an exact finite certificate about a concrete linear dynamical system.
status_note: The threshold-production gap is explicit in the 2014 primary theorem, the imported 2015 survey and Noubissie’s April 2025 manuscript. The checked growth theorem bounds the number of exceptional indices, and the May 2026 preprint imposes a unique-dominant-root hypothesis; neither provides the required total algorithm for arbitrary simple recurrences. A bounded search on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. This is dated source-open evidence with bounded current-status checking, not a proof of present openness or an independent verification of all cited arguments.
review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 2026-09-16; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

progress.text: Ouaknine and Worrell decide Ultimate Positivity for simple rational recurrences of every order, while explicitly recording that their algorithm does not in general produce a threshold.
The separate Positivity theorem handles simple recurrences through order nine and explains why arbitrary-order threshold computation would yield the stronger all-time decision result.
The imported survey formulates the remaining effective-threshold gap beyond the established low-order cases, using nonnegativity throughout.
Noubissie explicitly discusses the missing threshold and proves an effective cardinality bound for exceptional growth indices. The checked statement bounds their number rather than their positions.
Li’s preprint gives sufficient conditions under a unique-dominant-root assumption. The checked statement does not claim the general witness-output algorithm.

importance.reason: A substantial effectivity question tied to simple-recurrence Positivity and Skolem decidability, beyond merely improving a complexity bound. The known general ultimate-positivity decision procedure does not supply its witness, exposing a foundational algorithmic gap with verification consequences.

sentences: A simple rational linear recurrence has a characteristic polynomial with distinct roots and a finite exact description.
The question asks for an algorithm that produces an index beyond which every term is nonnegative whenever such an index exists.
Any sufficient index is accepted, with no requirement that it be minimal or small.
Ultimate Positivity itself is already decidable for this class, but the checked general algorithm does not compute the threshold and later cardinality bounds do not locate the final exception.
A general effective threshold would close a gap between eventual guarantees and finite witnesses and would decide all-time Positivity for simple recurrences.

definitions: An input explicitly lists \(k\ge1\), rational coefficients \(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1}\), and rational initial values \(u_0,\ldots,u_{k-1}\). For \(n\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), define \[u_{n+k}=\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_j u_{n+j},\qquad p(X)=X^k-\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}a_jX^j.\] The input is required to have a squarefree characteristic polynomial: \(p\) has no repeated complex roots, equivalently \(\gcd(p,p')=1\) over \(\mathbb Q[X]\). This effectively checkable representation covers every simple sequence via its minimal characteristic polynomial; minimum recurrence length is not itself an input requirement. A possible zero root contributes only a finite initial part and may be handled explicitly; allowing it does not extend the unresolved tail problem beyond the usual nonzero-root source convention. Every rational is given by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, and finite lists have explicit delimiters. Non-squarefree or malformed descriptions may be rejected as invalid inputs. Distinct roots may have equal moduli or root-of-unity ratios, and there is no promise of a unique dominant root. The recurrence coefficients are constant, not polynomials in the index. Nonnegative means \(u_n\ge0\), so zeros are allowed and the identically zero input admits \(N=0\). The output is a tagged \(\mathrm{NO}\) or an explicitly written binary natural number. The algorithm is uniform across all finite input lengths, uses no oracle or random error, and has no required time bound. Rational and integer presentations give the same target: multiplication by the positive factor \(D^{n+1}\), where \(D\) clears the input denominators, converts to integer initial values and integer coefficients while preserving signs, thresholds and distinctness of characteristic roots.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that the specified total output procedure exists, or prove that no such computable procedure exists. A positive answer must provide an algorithm and prove that each natural-number output bounds every negative term of that input, and that NO is returned precisely when no threshold exists. An algorithm required to halt only on ultimately nonnegative simple inputs is equally sufficient, together with the already established simple-case decision theorem and a Lean-checked justification of the equivalence. Any valid threshold is acceptable; neither minimality nor a prescribed asymptotic size is required. A nonconstructive existence proof for each individual threshold, or an algorithm returning only a yes/no ultimate-positivity answer, does not meet the witness-output requirement.

source_formulation.text: For an ultimately nonnegative simple linear recurrence of arbitrary order, compute an index after which all terms are nonnegative; the general decision procedure in the source does not produce this threshold.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the source question

context_blocks.text: Every yes-instance has at least one threshold by definition. The issue is whether one algorithm can obtain a valid threshold from each finite recurrence description. The target permits generous overestimates: there is no requirement to find the last negative term or an optimal bound. The requirement to compute a witness remains meaningful even with unlimited finite running time.

Simple recurrences have distinct characteristic roots, so the polynomial factors associated with repeated roots are absent. Nevertheless, multiple equally large oscillating contributions can nearly cancel at late indices. Restricting to a unique largest-modulus root would remove part of the source question.

The 2014 general simple-case theorem decides whether an eventual threshold exists, without computing it. Its proof uses noneffective Diophantine bounds; this explains a limit of that particular algorithm and does not prove that thresholds are uncomputable. The source explicitly identifies producing thresholds as the additional unresolved task.

The low-order result decides all-time Positivity for simple recurrences through order nine. The source distinguishes that effective result from the arbitrary-order decision theorem for Ultimate Positivity. A general threshold procedure would also decide all-time Positivity for the simple class, so completing this witness task would settle a significant associated decision problem.

Noubissie’s 2025 manuscript retains the threshold gap and gives an effective bound on how many indices violate a specified growth inequality. A bound on the number of exceptions does not locate the final exception: even a set with one element can place that element arbitrarily far out. The stated theorem therefore does not supply the threshold requested here.

The May 2026 preprint supplies sufficient conditions for polynomial-coefficient recurrences with a unique dominant root. Its unrestricted order parameter does not remove that root hypothesis or make its sufficient test a total procedure for every simple constant-coefficient recurrence. It is recorded as a restricted preprint result, not a resolution of this card.
